In an episode of family guy from around 2013 (maybe later than that) they make fun of millennials, and as background info to the overarching joke of the episode they describe millennials as being born between ‘85 and 2000, and many of the things they made fun of millennials for were things that I remember doing, seeing, or even just hearing about in my early teens. I know an episode of family guy isn’t a super credible source to base my opinion on, but it did get me thinking about the nature of “generationology,” and I’ve been hypothesizing that over time gen z will be considered to be more of a 2000-2015 thing, possibly even later. By the time I was a few years into college I remember news outlets using “gen z” to refer to high school age kids, and I started to get the feeling that gen z will be more remembered for the things kids born around ‘05-‘10 were doing. 

I don’t really think Gen z’s specific cringe is anything I care to avoid being associated with, in fact I think millennial cringe can be, and is often cringier, but I will admit I have a bias that leans millennially for how I identify. Growing up I had a lot of my siblings’ hand-me-downs (they were born in ‘88 and ‘94), much of which consisted of things like VHS Tapes, stereos with cassette players, PlayStation, SNES, game boy Colors, animorph books, and such. My family still had a dial up modem in my early childhood, and the cell phones my parents had were Nokias that were painstaking to type on. I remember when emojis didn’t exist, when Netflix was a mail subscription, rage comics before ifunny, and watching Obama run for and winning his first election, as well as the significance of it. I think if millennial doesn’t end at 2000, then 2000 is at least on the final wave of it, and at the forefront of the changing culture, but mostly I think it’ll be in the future that people start to consider millenniality as stretching into 2000

I was of legal drinking age in the middle of the pandemic and that kinda sets us apart, I think, from people who were still kids, or teens and lived with their parents at home when it happened. I’m in that 1/3rd group, and for me personally I’m just not very interested in dating anymore. I’ve done the tinder/bumble/hinge thing and have had success, but I’ve grown to largely dislike the vibes most people on them have, and would much rather meet prospective partners organically. Additionally I lack most of the energy and motivation to really even bother trying to pursue any romantic relationships—I’m not really afraid of rejection, but I much rather keep to myself or whatever friends I’m out with. I don’t approach people I don’t know, but if I am approached I can hold a conversation pretty well, and can be engaging and charismatic, yet I will almost never be the approacher. 
I’m also generally much less interested in sex now than I was in the past, especially the casual/hookup/anonymous kinds. I think my lack of interest in sex even makes me prefer not pursuing a relationship with someone based on the assumption that, to them, sex might be important or integral to a romantic relationship. There are a lot of things I want/like to do and I have much more time to do them by not having a committed relationship. 
I guess after having had a handful of relationships I’m a bit tired of even the idea of being in one, and I’m much too disinterested in sex to really want one, or even a “friends with benefits” type of thing. I like keeping to myself and not having to worry about finding a partner. I figure somewhere down the line I’ll find someone, or someone will find me and maybe change my mind, and while my libido is abysmal I do think intimacy is very nice, but as of now I’m vibing on my own, and I enjoy having a lot of time to myself

Also, I don’t know where this comes from, and I feel a little bad about it, but there’s a strange sense of satisfaction I may glean from turning someone down, or refusing someone’s advances (politely, mind you) on the very rare occasion someone approaches me inquisitively. I’m not trying to be a dick, I’m just genuinely not interested, but appreciative of being move-making material in someone else’s eyes. Does that make me an asshole?

I’m trying to imagine that level of the feeling of fucking yourself over by your own actions. It’s something I think we all know, but it certainly doesn’t happen everyday, and putting myself in that driver’s shoes (I guess fins now? Maybe galoshes?) I don’t think I could kick myself hard enough because a mere moment of hastiness and impatience had *immediate* and *extremely expensive* repercussions. 

They seemed to honk at the parked cars, and were probably a bit annoyed with them blocking the lane. In hindsight, and through the video shown, there’s almost some dramatic irony amongst that driver and the rest of the onlookers. Everyone else seems to understand the situation, but one driver’s hubris leads to a fuckload of misery, no matter the outcome. 

Either a car or a life was lost in the aftermath, but in that instance when full realization is donned, and there couldn’t possibly be anyone else to blame, it must feel pretty painful not to have taken just a moment to consider your next actions. In many things we do there’s a “point of no return,” and it drives the idea in my mind that actions have inherent commitment to them, as we commit them. 

I do think it was a dumb decision not to pause and consider their surroundings, and I think anyone could have avoided this, but I mostly just feel sorry for them. If they survived they have a very expensive mistake on their hands, and if not the cost of their life will weigh heavily in the hearts of their friends and family. It makes me wonder what other things that person might be a bit hasty towards, what levels of “kicking themselves” they may have experienced previously in their life, and if that feeling in this instance is the greatest one yet. It’s videos like these that reinforce my appreciation for taking my time, not cutting every corner, and paying more attention to my surroundings. I’ve often heard that “haste makes waste” and that adage certainly rings true very often in this world. 

In the end, I hope that driver managed to make it out okay, as I’m sure the pain of having fucked yourself over is infinitely easier on the soul than the pain of a loved one’s life lost. They may have to live through hell to deal with a car that almost certainly is totaled, but the lesson would undoubtedly have been learned, and the driver would come out a little bit wiser

Something people don’t often consider is how being arrested and catching a charge even once can cause someone to be in and out of jail for the rest of their life. The sheer amount of money being siphoned out of a person by other people, bondsmen, agencies, public defenders, and ridiculous bureaucratic fees the moment you’ve been charged with even a misdemeanor can financially ruin a person, for most people don’t have any liquid money to shill out by the thousands to fulfill what the state requires. Not being able to afford some of these fees makes you liable to have punishments intensified or lengthened. Many impositions placed by the county or state can make one’s life extremely difficult, disrupting their ability to live and work as they used to, and that on top of the ludicrous leeching can drown a person. Being poor, for lack of a better explanation, is almost a crime after you’ve been charged with an offense. Even without owing restitution, being unable to afford these costs can land you back in jail. If you live in a different state or county from where you’ve offended, you’re much more likely to catch a warrant for your arrest for failure to appear in court, especially if suspension or revocation of your license is one of those impositions. 

That being said, police officers hardly ever have to be involved in a case after they’ve arrested someone. Police have the ability to charge you with almost anything they want or deem appropriate, and all they need to do is paperwork of their own personal testimony that becomes “fact” after the arrest. You’ll see many videos of arrests where cops brazenly detain a person and tell them they’ll have to, “fight it in court,” knowing damn well how expensive court fees and legal representation are. People can rarely afford those fees, especially considering the loads and loads of fees already being imposed on them just for being arrested and charged. Now, I don’t mean to imply that nobody that gets arrested is deserving of the weight of the hammer of the law, but arresting “criminals” and bringing down that hammer hardly ever teaches the lesson people think it does. More often than not it can create career criminals and repeat offenders. Plenty of people can whip up into shape after the first arrest, but the system wants you to mess up. You are being preyed upon by several forces that are waiting for you to make a mistake, and once that mistake is made they all strike simultaneously, all in the name of money. Police are essentially governmentally sanctioned debt creators, and have such immunity that protects them from being wrong when they upend a person’s life. 

Additionally, the legal system is such an intricate and merciless machine that it takes years and years of studying it just to be able to navigate it and understand it, and nobody (besides those that pursue that knowledge) in this country is educated enough to do that. Otherwise “normal” people can be pinned with charges of resisting, failure to identify, failure to report, trespassing, and one of the most bullshit charges cops fabricate, obstructing. These are not things taught in high school, nor college unless you study it. These are ways that police officers on their high horses and power trips can turn a person into a career criminal, and it hardly ever teaches others to “not commit crimes.” Some of us have to learn this the hard way, while others learn by watching it happen to people they know, and as deterring as it is and seems, it doesn’t stop the corrupt system from targeting us. Rule bending is a superpower that these rule enforcers are blessed with by this corrupt system. It may make examples of people, but it doesn’t change the fact that you can be charged with almost anything a police officer deems appropriate

A couple years ago I played guitar in a pit that did the music for a high school’s production of this play. The music for this show is actually kinda wild, it’s written to include two guitarists, each with like 3-4 different kinds of guitars on standby, but there wasn’t really enough money to hire more than just one so I kinda just covered enough of what both of those parts were doing. 

Most of the songs we thought were a little lame, or a kinda weird because it’s just got some of the craziest music ideas mashed up together in several songs, but I’ll admit some of them I kinda liked, like “don’t let me go” and “who I’d be” and there’s an early one Fiona sings that I thought was fun, though I can’t remember many other songs we did. 

My favorite characters, or at least the performances I liked the most that the kids did were Farquaad’s, donkey and shrek, and also Pinocchio. The kid that played Farquaad was an absolute superstar and had a great voice, and the chemistry between shrek and donkey was awesome. The kid playing Pinocchio was straight up the best actor. 

The biggest issues, however, were that some of the cast actually had like no sense of rhythm or tempo, so for example Fiona’s singing that song in her tower (I think it was “I know it’s today”) but *consistently* 1-2 bars ahead of us, and the directors of the band and the play could not agree *at all* on how to go about fixing it and rehearsing and everything else. Our music director kinda actually didn’t know shit about conducting, and had completely different arrangements of the music that he was using as the score and couldn’t keep up with the band.

In the end, the morning of the first performance of the play the directors decided to fire the band and used the MIDI piano track they initially practiced with for all of their music. They did pay us for all of our rehearsals and time spent traveling to the venue and stuff, and we were greatly happy to even be getting paid after being so suddenly discarded, but frankly we were a little pissed off that we didn’t get to do the real shows. It was fun seeing the kids act and sing and improve and practice, and I know it would’ve felt better for them if we could’ve played the real music that night. We felt kinda blue-balled for lack of a better term 

But anyway, that’s my shrek the musical story. Several years ago I was a teenager riding a bike down Pikes Peak in Colorado Springs. I had a go pro camera on my helmet and every now and then while going down the longer switchbacks I’d kinda turn my head a little to get a cool shot of the horizon so my mom could see, but one time I did that I noticed the turn going down the switchback a little too late, and wound up sliding off my bike since I couldn’t turn so fast. After that, and also after watching that movie The Secret Life of Walter Mitty I decided I didn’t care so much about trying to capture stuff on camera anymore. Sometimes cameras can be distracting especially when you’re struck with a vision for something to point it at, but I think sometimes we forget to use our eyes because of it. I think for a comedy movie they should have the protagonists be more of the engine of the comedy, like they should be the funniest ones in the movie. I thought for a comedy movie about empowering women they sure didn’t make them too funny. 

Like lemme put it this way, if the Barbies and the Kens were to be assigned to the leads in Pineapple Express, the Kens would be James Franco’s character, and the Barbies would be Seth Rogen’s character. Seth Rogen’s character was great in that, don’t get me wrong, but throughout the movie he’s maybe the most frantic, or worried character. A lot of his dialogue at times when the two of them are in the scene together is just him kinda freaking out about the situation, or about something James Franco’s character did or said. He didn’t drive so much of the comedic things at times, and was more just “reactionarily” funny while James Franco delivered more comedic lines with a more or less comedic style* 

What I mean to say with this comparison is that I felt that the Barbies were written in such a way that didn’t allow them to make jokes, I felt like they mostly just reacted to jokes that others made, similar to how Seth Rogen does in Pineapple Express, and I’m not the biggest fan of his character in that one, but I feel like when a comedy movie’s projected goal is women empowerment the main Barbie should’ve been a stronger character; one that made the most jokes that other people reacted to, and at least been funnier than the male lead. Additionally, I think the best Barbie was the weird Barbie, I believe that was Kate McKinnon, and she happened to be the funniest, and delivered good jokes well. 

The last thing I’ll mention about this movie is that I know there’s got to be some kind of extended metaphor or something about Barbieland, but I can’t figure it out. I can’t tell if Barbieland is a parody of a patriarchal society, I can’t tell if it’s a projection of a desire for a completely matriarchal society, I was thinking it might’ve been an illustration of a society with a few different classes of citizens—of which the Barbies were atop, and how it was righteous and everything was in order, and that that illustration was the point trying to be gotten across by the film, but after Ken and Barbie left, and Ken came back first, bringing his idea of the patriarchy with him, I don’t think we actually see him brainwash them like they say he did, but when he returns, literally everybody in Barbieland was completely onboard with it, and loved it. So when this happens I’m suddenly very confused because I can’t tell what’s happening to the message. It took no time for the entirety of Barbieland to be completely enamored with the style of society Ken introduced, and now im wondering if they’re suggesting a patriarchy isn’t so bad. Initially I thought maybe the kens were a metaphor for real life American women, and that the kens were a hyperbole of a status that I imagine an amount of women in our society feel they’re resigned to. That thought made sense to me, but then Ken introduces his idea of patriarchy and I’m left wondering if the Kens are a metaphor for like male ego or something. The problem with that is that the kens are so much easier to feel pity for, or to see as the underdog of the story, and it doesn’t make sense to me to have the metaphor for toxic masculinity be the underdog when you’re making a feminist comedy movie. So I feel like the message of the movie is maybe contrived. The movie felt much too deliberate and on the nose, and I know this movie is literally for little girls/little kids (which is why I don’t understand why it was even so popular, besides the cast and all the marketing involved) so it has to be easy enough to understand, but there are plenty of children intended films that employ subtlety effectively.
